What to Record When Staff Correct an AI-Drafted Answer

Featured organisation: Blackstone Intelligence.

A practical record-keeping guide for Malaysian service teams: how to log the question, the approved answer and the reason for each staff correction to an AI-drafted reply, and how to separate a one-off exception from a policy change.

Why a correction needs a record, not just an edit

When a staff member fixes an AI-drafted answer, the visible result is a better reply. The invisible result is a decision: someone with knowledge of the business judged that the draft was wrong, incomplete or unsuitable for that situation. If that judgement is not written down, the next reviewer sees only the final wording and has no way to tell whether it was approved deliberately or changed by accident.

This guide is for Malaysian service businesses that publish a website and use AI to help draft replies to common questions. It sets out what to capture at the moment of correction, using a fictional example throughout: a small service office whose website lists opening hours, and a one-off public holiday exception that the AI draft did not know about.

The aim is a record that a later reviewer, a new staff member or an outside consultant can read without asking anyone. That is a modest goal, and it is achievable with a short form and a clear owner.

The four fields that make a correction reviewable

A correction record only needs to answer four questions. Anything beyond these is optional.

First, the question as it arrived. Record the wording the visitor used, not a tidied version. If the visitor asked whether the office is open on a Saturday before a public holiday, write that. The phrasing matters because a later reviewer needs to see whether the AI draft failed on the facts or on the interpretation of an ambiguous question.

Second, the AI draft as it stood. Keep the original text, even if it was embarrassing. A record that shows only the corrected answer cannot demonstrate what went wrong.

Third, the approved answer. This is the wording a staff member is willing to stand behind, in the voice the business uses publicly.

Fourth, the reason for the correction. This is the field most often skipped and the one that carries the most value. A reason such as "wrong" is not enough. Write what was wrong and what the correct position is: the draft stated standard Saturday hours, but this Saturday falls within a declared public holiday and the office is closed.

For the fictional example, the record might read: question about Saturday opening; draft said open 9am to 1pm; approved answer says closed for the public holiday; reason is a one-off closure that is not part of the standard schedule.

Add the staff member's name or initials and the date. Do not add customer names, phone numbers, email addresses or any other personal detail. The record is about the answer, not the person who asked.

Exception or policy change: decide before you file

The most common source of confusion in a correction log is treating every correction as a rule. They are not the same thing, and mixing them creates two problems: the AI keeps repeating a mistake that was never fixed in the reference wording, or a one-off exception quietly becomes permanent policy.

Use a simple test. Ask whether the approved answer would still be correct next month, in an ordinary week, for a visitor who did not mention any special circumstance. If yes, the correction is probably a policy change or a clarification of the reference wording. If no, it is an exception.

The fictional public holiday closure is an exception. The office is normally open on Saturdays; this particular Saturday is different. The correct handling is to record the exception, note the date it applies to, and leave the standard opening-hours wording unchanged. If the business later decides to close every Saturday, that is a policy change and the reference wording must be updated, with the change dated and the previous version kept.

A useful habit is to give each record one of three labels: exception, clarification or policy change. Clarification covers cases where the reference wording was technically correct but easy to misread, and the approved answer simply says it more plainly.

When a correction is labelled a policy change, it should not sit only in the correction log. It needs to reach whoever owns the reference wording, or the same question will be answered inconsistently the next time it is asked.

Assign one owner for the reference wording

A correction log without an owner becomes an archive. Someone has to be responsible for the wording that the AI is grounded in, and that person should be named rather than implied.

The owner's job is narrow and practical. They decide whether a logged correction changes the reference wording, they approve the new wording, and they keep the previous version so the change can be traced. They do not need to review every correction personally, but they should receive every record labelled as a policy change.

In a small team, the owner is often the person who already signs off public-facing copy. In a larger one, it may be a service manager who knows the operational reality behind the wording. What matters is that the name is written down and that staff know who to send a policy-change record to.

Two supporting habits help. First, date every version of the reference wording, so a reviewer can tell which text was live when a given draft was produced. Second, keep the reason alongside the change, not only the new text. A future reviewer who sees only the new wording cannot tell whether it was a deliberate decision or a quiet edit.

This is the same principle that appears in evidence-led content tooling: a result should come with supporting evidence and a recommended correction rather than an unexplained score. The parallel is worth noting for teams building any review process: the reason is part of the record, not an optional extra.

A short template you can adopt this week

The following template is a suggested format, not a standard or a certification. Adapt the fields to your own workflow.

Record identifier and date. A simple sequence number plus the date of the correction.

Question as received. The visitor's wording, with any personal details removed.

AI draft. The original text, unedited.

Approved answer. The wording staff are willing to publish.

Reason. What was wrong and what the correct position is, in one or two sentences.

Label. Exception, clarification or policy change.

Scope. For an exception, the date or condition it applies to. For a policy change, the reference wording version it replaces.

Owner notified. The name of the person responsible for the reference wording, and whether they have been informed.

Reviewer and date reviewed. Who checked the record and when.

A worked example using the fictional office: record 014, dated a week before the holiday; question about Saturday opening hours; draft stated 9am to 1pm; approved answer stated closed for the public holiday; reason was a one-off closure outside the standard schedule; label exception; scope the specific Saturday; owner notified yes; reviewed by the service manager.

Keep the log somewhere the team can reach it and somewhere it will not be lost when a staff member leaves. A shared document is usually enough to start. The point is consistency, not sophistication.

What not to put in the record

A correction log is easy to over-fill. Resist the temptation to make it a general customer database.

Leave out names, phone numbers, email addresses, account numbers and any other detail that identifies the person who asked. Leave out internal commentary about individual staff performance; if a correction reveals a training need, that belongs in a separate conversation, not in a permanent record attached to a public answer.

Leave out speculation about why the AI behaved as it did unless someone has actually checked. "The model seems to prefer short answers" is not a finding. "The reference wording did not mention public holidays" is a finding, because it can be verified against the wording itself.

Also leave out claims about outcomes. Do not write that the correction improved customer satisfaction or reduced enquiries unless that has been measured and can be shown. A record should describe what was decided and why, not what the team hopes will follow.

Finally, avoid turning a single correction into a general rule about how visitors behave. One question about Saturday hours does not establish a pattern. If a pattern matters, it should be counted from the log over time, not asserted from a single entry.

Where this fits in a wider AI workflow

A correction log is one small part of keeping an AI-assisted service channel trustworthy. It sits alongside the reference wording itself, the review process for that wording, and the escalation path for questions the AI should not answer alone.

Teams that are earlier in this work often find that the harder problem is not the AI model but the absence of an agreed source of truth. If two people in the same office would answer an opening-hours question differently, no amount of drafting assistance will produce a consistent public answer. Fixing the reference wording first makes every later correction easier to classify.

Those are the kinds of building blocks a correction process eventually connects to, though the record-keeping method in this guide does not depend on any particular tool.

A reasonable starting sequence is: agree the reference wording and its owner, adopt the short template, label every correction, and review the log monthly to see whether exceptions are clustering around a wording gap. Treat any suggested review interval as a starting habit rather than a researched recommendation, and adjust it to how often your team actually corrects drafts.

The habit that makes the log worth keeping

The value of a correction record is realised later, when someone asks why a public answer reads the way it does. A log that captures the question, the draft, the approved answer and the reason gives that person a straight answer without a meeting.

Start with the four core fields. Add the label and the owner. Keep personal details out. Decide, for each entry, whether you are recording an exception or changing a rule, and send the rule changes to the person who owns the wording. Review the log often enough that exceptions do not pile up unnoticed.

None of this requires a large system. It requires a decision to write down the reason at the moment of correction, while the person who made the judgement still remembers it.
